body:
DESIGNED WITH MYK IN CHAT, 2026-08-19. Depends on T186 (the federation channel model). This
ticket is the AGENT INTERFACE to it. Myk: "agent interfaces will be the primary way that this stuff
is used."

WHY MCP TOOLS AND NOT NEW JSON-RPC METHODS. MCP's sanctioned extension point is TOOLS. A custom
method (`federation/open`) never appears in `tools/list`, so a model cannot discover it and a strict
client may reject it — this repo already paid for that lesson with `server/discover`. So the protocol
surface stays `initialize` / `tools/list` / `tools/call` / `server/discover`, and federation arrives
as tools.

WHAT THE OFFER TOOL IS ACTUALLY FOR — this is the ticket's strongest argument. Today
`GET /:mount/federate` demands the OPERATOR token (http.ts, the `federate` case). The same token
registers root law, mints grants, drops containers, and reads everything. So "let me federate with
you" currently costs a peer the ENTIRE STORE. A container-scoped offer replaces that with a key to
one container.

AUTHORITY IS A CONTAINER-SCOPED GRANT, NOT THE OPERATOR ROLE (Myk's correction in chat; the first
draft said operator-only and he rejected it). SPEC 28 says trust is a property of a CONTAINER and
multitenancy is a goal, so re-centralizing on the operator would defeat the model this arc exists to
build. The shape mirrors T174 exactly — a verb in the grant vocabulary, scoped:

    loam grant --verb=federate --container=<id> <subject>

The operator holds it at root by construction rather than as a special case.

THE TOOLS:

1. `loam_federate_offer`   {container, note?} -> {address, token}
   Mints a CONTAINER-SCOPED token. Replaces handing over the operator token.
2. `loam_federate_connect` {source, into, prefix, bless?} -> {channel, accepted, refused, bound[], parked[]}
   One call for both directions: an offer's address, or a public source's address.
3. `loam_federate_status`  {channel?} -> {peer, into, prefix, receiving, blessing, lastSyncedAt,
   consecutiveFailures, parked[], bound[]}
   This is the H9 answer: a channel that quietly stopped must be distinguishable from a peer with
   nothing new.
4. `loam_federate_set`     {channel, receiving?, blessing?, resolve?: {name, as|supersede}, curse?}
   The reversible controls only.
5. `loam_federate_drop`    {channel} -> a STAGED drop, never a purge. See below.

DROP IS STAGED BY THE AGENT AND CONFIRMED BY A HUMAN, AND THE SECOND PHASE IS STRUCTURALLY OUT OF
THE AGENT'S REACH. Myk: "How can we make it so that there is always a user confirm step on drop and
it can never fire on its own?"

The answer is not a flag and not client-side elicitation (which trusts the client, and an
agent-driven client can auto-approve). It is that the two surfaces authenticate DIFFERENTLY:
- MCP callers are a `TokenIdentity` (bearer / OAuth connector).
- The admin page sits behind `SessionGate` — a browser session cookie (admin.ts, session.ts).
A connector token cannot become a session. So:

- `loam_federate_drop` STAGES: it returns a staged-drop id, a URL, an expiry, and a TWO-SIDED
  PREVIEW (what would be purged; which named peers survive). It purges NOTHING.
- The purge path REFUSES a `TokenIdentity` outright. Not a checked flag — the deleting code requires
  a session-authenticated actor. An agent calling drop a thousand times purges nothing.
- Staged drops EXPIRE (~10 min), so a stale stage cannot be confirmed into something else later.
- THE PREVIEW IS RECOMPUTED AT CONFIRM TIME, and a confirm whose recomputed preview differs from the
  staged one REFUSES and re-stages. Otherwise an agent stages a small drop, the data grows, and the
  human approves something larger than they read — H7, at the interaction layer.
- One stage per channel; re-staging replaces.

The generalization is worth keeping beyond this ticket: AGENTS STAGE IRREVERSIBLE ACTS, HUMANS
CONFIRM THEM.

RAILS, red first:
1. A holder of a container-scoped `federate` grant offers THAT container; a holder scoped to another
   container is refused, and the refusal is the existing uniform shape (no new oracle).
2. An offer's token reads that container's deltas and NOT the store's — a bystander container's
   deltas are absent from what the offer serves. Two-sided.
3. `loam_federate_connect` through an offer token reaches the same state as the CLI path from T186.
4. `loam_federate_status` reports `lastSyncedAt` and `consecutiveFailures`, and a peer that has been
   unreachable is reported as unreachable rather than as nothing new.
5. `loam_federate_drop` over MCP purges NOTHING. Assert at the BYTES: after the call, every delta the
   preview named is still present.
6. The purge path refuses a `TokenIdentity` even when handed a valid staged-drop id — the gate is
   the identity kind, not the id.
7. A confirm whose recomputed preview differs from the staged preview refuses and re-stages.
8. An expired stage cannot be confirmed.
9. The completed purge (session-confirmed) is TWO-SIDED: the channel's deltas are gone at the bytes
   AND a named second channel's data still reads.
10. The operator holds `federate` at root without an explicit grant.

TIER: MYK'S MERGE, and he pre-blessed it in chat on 2026-08-19 — "you have my blessing to merge this
one when it's ready, as long as you are delivering what we've discussed here and no big surprises
come up." The purge widening still owes its one-line statement of what can now be deleted that could
not before, and any DEVIATION from the design above voids the pre-blessing rather than bending it.

WHY FIVE TOOLS AND NOT ONE `federate` TOOL TAKING CLI-SHAPED ARGUMENTS (asked by Myk, 2026-08-19;
answer recorded because the next reader will re-ask it). A single passthrough tool is smaller and
mirrors the CLI, and it defeats this ticket'''s central safety property.

TOOLS ARE THE UNIT OF CONSENT, not merely of capability. MCP clients apply policy PER TOOL —
auto-approve one, always-ask another, deny a third. Five tools let an operator auto-approve
`status` while `drop` asks every time. ONE tool collapses that to allow-or-deny-all-federation, so
the choice becomes an agent that cannot read channel health, or an agent that can reach drop. The
staged-confirm boundary above survives at the server, but the client-side layer that makes it
ergonomic is gone, and it is gone somewhere the server cannot compensate.

Three supporting reasons, descending: (a) tool descriptions are the model'''s only documentation, and
a CLI-passthrough tool documents no flag grammar anywhere in the protocol; (b) five `inputSchema`
objects are validated by the client BEFORE the call, while `args: string[]` validates nothing and
turns every mistake into a server-side parse refusal; (c) a passthrough couples the wire to CLI flag
syntax permanently, making a flag rename a breaking change for every connector.

The concern behind the question is real — a store that grows a tool per feature ends with forty. The
answer is a small, sharply-named set with no overlap, which is what five is: one per intent. Do NOT
merge `status` into `set` either; a client should be able to grant read without granting write.


loam_federate_offer IS BLOCKED ON T196'S DECISION. Measured 2026-08-19, before building it.

The tool's whole value is minting a CONTAINER-SCOPED token so a peer stops needing the operator
token. But there is no runtime mint to hang it on: `serve` builds its token table once, at boot —

    const tokenEntries = Object.entries(options.tokens).map(([token, identity]) => [sha(token), identity]);

— from static configuration, and nothing anywhere adds to it later. The OAuth doors do mint
credentials (connector client ids, access tokens), but those authenticate an INBOUND connector; a
peer pulling from `GET /:mount/federate` presents a BEARER token, and that table is fixed.

So `offer` cannot be delivered without deciding WHERE A RUNTIME-ISSUED FEDERATION CREDENTIAL LIVES —
the same question T196 is blocked on, from the other side. T196 asks where the token a channel USES
is kept; `offer` asks where the token a channel HANDS OUT is kept. One decision answers both, and
this repo never puts a secret in the ground (a pen's seed lives in the home's config; the operator
seed is 0600 and never printed).

Building it anyway would mean inventing credential storage on Myk's behalf, which VOIDS the
pre-blessing rather than bending it. So: four tools are buildable now, and `offer` waits.

WHAT THIS COSTS IN THE MEANTIME, said plainly: federating still requires handing a peer the operator
token, with everything that token can do. The `federate` VERB is landed and scopes what a holder may
do INSIDE this store, which is real — but it does not yet replace the credential a peer needs to pull.
Do not describe the operator-token problem as solved.
title: Federation over MCP — five tools, a container-scoped grant, and a drop an agent cannot fire
